clinicalPearls: A rare, aggressive form of systemic mastocytosis defined by a high proportion of atypical mast cells in the bone marrow
Circulating mast cells may or may not be present (classical versus aleukaemic variants)
Presents with rapidly progressive organ dysfunction, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly and severe mediator symptoms
Serum tryptase is typically very high
It carries a poor prognosis with short survival in many cases
Management involves cytoreductive and KIT-targeted therapies and consideration of stem cell transplantation, alongside aggressive mediator control
reference.pathophysiology: Mast cell leukaemia is the most aggressive category of systemic mastocytosis, characterised by extensive proliferation of atypical, often immature, clonal mast cells that heavily infiltrate the bone marrow and impair normal haematopoiesis. Although KIT mutations are common, the mutation profile can differ from indolent disease and influences response to targeted therapy. The massive mast cell burden causes both marrow failure with cytopenias and organ infiltration, and profuse mediator release producing severe systemic symptoms.
additionalDifferentials: Other systemic mastocytosis with an associated haematological neoplasm
additionalInvestigations: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with mast cell quantification and immunophenotyping
Blood film for circulating mast cells
Staging of organ involvement and assessment for transplant candidacy
redFlags: Rapidly progressive cytopenias and organ failure
Very high mast cell burden on marrow
Features of an associated haematological neoplasm
reference.prognosis: Mast cell leukaemia has a poor prognosis with short median survival in many series, though newer KIT-targeted agents and transplantation may improve outcomes in selected patients.
pitfalls: Delaying marrow examination in rapidly progressive mastocytosis
Assuming standard KIT-targeted therapy will work regardless of mutation profile
Underestimating the risk of catastrophic mediator release
management: KIT-targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors (midostaurin or avapritinib) directed by the KIT mutation profile
Cytoreductive chemotherapy such as cladribine to reduce the mast cell burden
Consider allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation in eligible patients
Aggressive mediator control with H1- and H2-antihistamines, mast cell stabilisers and self-injectable adrenaline for anaphylaxis
Supportive care for marrow failure, including transfusion of blood products and treatment of infection
Manage through a specialist haematology multidisciplinary team with transplant assessment
